item.description:
Check the team’s overlap hours before you apply

If a remote job asks for “four hours of overlap,” find out where those hours fall in your day before you plan around them.

A question you can send
“Which hours and days do I need to overlap with the team? Is there a fixed block, or can I choose the hours? Does the window follow a local time zone or stay fixed in UTC?”

Example
Say a role requires 09:00–13:00 New York time. In Berlin, that’s 15:00–19:00 on March 2, 2027, and 14:00–18:00 on March 16. The US and the EU move their clocks on different dates that month.

Try it on your calendar
Make a test event in the team’s time zone and view it in yours. Check a date on either side of the next clock change and compare the hours with your actual commitments. Google Calendar instructions.

item.description:
Before starting a remote task, agree what “finished” means

Try this when a request sounds like “make onboarding clearer.” Write a short proposal and ask the requester to confirm it.

Fictional example — a customer onboarding checklist
Deliverable: An English checklist for new customers using the web app.

Proposed acceptance criteria:
• Covers creating an account, inviting a teammate and creating a first project.
• Each step matches the labels and sequence checked in the test workspace.
• Missing instructions or blocked steps are flagged for the reviewer.

Scope: Mobile instructions and translations are excluded from this draft.
Reviewer: Customer Success lead.
Handoff: Draft for review; publishing requires approval.

Copy-and-adapt message
“Before I start, can we confirm the deliverable, the checks it must pass, what is outside scope and who will review it? I propose [criteria]. Is [date, time and time zone] suitable for the review?”

Apply it: Put the agreed criteria in the task itself. Before handing over, check each one and note anything still unresolved. If scope changes, confirm the revised criteria.

Atlassian’s guide explains acceptance criteria as verifiable conditions for completion. The example above is our suggested practice exercise.

item.title: Practice a support reply without guessing the outcome Applying for remote custom
item.description:
Practice a support reply without guessing the outcome

Applying for remote customer support? Try this writing exercise.

Fictional scenario
A customer says: “My delivery is late. I needed it today.” You can check tracking, but have no verified delivery date.

Example reply
“I’m sorry your order hasn’t arrived when you needed it. Could you share your order reference in this private support channel so I can find the shipment? I’ll check its tracking status, then explain the next steps available under our delivery policy.”

Review your draft:
• Ask for a useful detail and explain why you need it.
• State a next step you can actually take.
• Avoid promising a delivery date or refund you haven’t verified.
• Add a follow-up time only if you can commit to it.

Adapt the reply to the product, your permissions and the employer’s policies.

Further reading: GitLab’s ticket-response guide covers explaining your request and continuing to help.

item.title: Ask how a remote team handles changing priorities A question to try in your next
item.description:
Ask how a remote team handles changing priorities

A question to try in your next interview:
“Can you walk me through a recent project where priorities changed? How was the decision communicated, and how did the team adjust?”

Useful follow-ups
• Who decided what to stop working on?
• Where were the new priorities recorded?
• What happened when a teammate was offline?

Recommendation: ask for a recent example, then compare the process with how you prefer to work. If the answer stays general, ask: “What did that look like on the last project?”

A note template to use afterwards:
Decision owner: [who]
Updates recorded in: [where]
Expected response time: [when]
Still unclear: [one follow-up]

item.title: Before deleting duplicates, define what one row means A practical spreadsheet ex
item.description:
Before deleting duplicates, define what one row means

A practical spreadsheet exercise for remote operations, admin and customer-support roles:

Fictional example
Your table is designed to hold one row per order:
Customer 42 | Order A | Paid
Customer 42 | Order B | Paid

The customer repeats, but these are different orders. Removing rows based only on the customer would lose a valid order.

Try this workflow
1. Work on a copy and keep the original export.
2. Write the rule: “One row represents one order.” For another dataset, that might be one ticket, payment or application.
3. Choose the matching key: here, Order ID. Investigate repeated IDs before deciding which records to keep.
4. In Google Sheets, select the full table, then use Data → Data cleanup → Remove duplicates. Check the header setting and choose the comparison columns deliberately.
5. Compare the result with the original and document what changed.

Google’s official instructions explain the column and header choices. The rule and example above are a suggested practice exercise.

A handoff note to adapt:
“Each row represents [unit]. I compared [columns], removed [confirmed duplicates], and flagged [unresolved cases].”

item.title: Replace “it doesn’t work” with a useful bug report Try this writing exercise if
item.description:
Replace “it doesn’t work” with a useful bug report

Try this writing exercise if you’re applying for support, QA or engineering roles.

Mozilla’s bug-reporting guide recommends precise steps, separate expected and actual results, and one issue per report. Keep observations separate from guesses about the cause.

A template to adapt
Title: [specific action + problem]
Environment: [app/browser version, device and OS]
Starting point: [setup or test data needed]
Steps: [one action per line]
Expected: [what should happen]
Actual: [what you observed]
Repeatability: [every time, sometimes, or not reproduced]
Evidence: [relevant screenshot or error text, with private data removed]

Fictional example
Title: Removing an item leaves the old cart total.
Steps: Add two demo items → remove one → check the total.
Expected: The total matches the remaining item.
Actual: The total still includes the removed item.

Practice check: Ask someone to follow your steps without a call. If they need missing setup details, add them. Use real observations when describing your own work.

item.title: Can a recruiter open your portfolio link? Try this check before sending an appli
item.description:
Can a recruiter open your portfolio link?

Try this check before sending an application:

1. Test the exact link.
For a public sample, open it in a private browser window where you are signed out. Check the file itself, not just the folder.

2. Choose the right audience.
In Google Drive, “Restricted” means access must be granted. “Anyone with the link” allows access without a Google sign-in; use it only for material you can safely share that widely. For a private sample, give the intended reviewer access instead.

3. Check the permission level.
Choose Viewer when editing is unnecessary. Check the parent folder too: broader folder permissions can carry through to the file.

4. Review what you are sending.
Use the correct version and remove confidential material. If your work account blocks external sharing, follow the employer’s upload instructions or use an approved alternative.

Example link label: “Customer onboarding sample — fictional scenario”.

Google Drive’s sharing guide explains the access settings.
